newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF to require I.D. in Eurobond tax law-sources.
newsitem.headline: MOF to require I.D. in Eurobond tax law-sources.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance has come up with a proposal that would continue to exempt foreigners from paying withholding taxes on income gains from such investments as Eurobonds on condition that the buyers identify themselves, industry sources said on Tuesday.
The sources, however, said the ministry would keep in mind the special characteristics of the Swiss market, which adheres to a strict rule of confidentiality.
In November, three major Swiss banks, Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corp and UBS, jointly submitted a petition urging MOF to reconsider its plan.
The industry sources said the Swiss banks are expected to present their counterproposal to MOF within several days.

MOF has already informed the Trade Ministry, financial industries and domestic borrowers that it is planning to submit its plan to the Liberal Democratic Party's tax panel for discussion, possibly on Wednesday, they said.
"According to MOF's plan, it will require identification from final investors," an official at the Trade Ministry said.
"Unless the final investors identify themselves, they will be required to pay the withholding tax," the official said.
The official said MOF will continue to impose a tax on foreign bonds which are issued by Japanese borrowers, including standard Eurobonds and Euroyen bonds held by Japanese investors.

MOF first raised the plan in early October, saying it wanted to repeal the law to close a loophole which gave tax breaks on Euroyen purchases to Japanese investors who buy the bonds through the overseas subsidiaries of Japanese firms.
A MOF study showed that about 80 percent of Euroyen bonds are held by Japanese investors. It said the law, which aims to encourage bond purchases by foreigners, has been abused.

"We heard a vague plan by the MOF that it would require identification," an official with an industry group, who did not wish to be identified, said. "We've been against MOF's idea because there is a danger the rule could affect the Eurobond market greatly."
MOF is expected to see the industry's reaction after it presents its plan to the panel and makes any final adjustments before it becomes law, they said.
"I strongly wish they (MOF's Tax Bureau) would not come up with a rule that would undermine the (Eurobond) market," a senior government official told Reuters.
